# Practice — Melting

Ten questions instantiated from the assessment guide. Objective 1 is covered by Q1–Q5; Objective 2 is
covered by Q6–Q10.

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 1
What is the melting point of pure water at standard pressure?
:::
::: tab Answer 1
0 °C.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 2
Give the melting point of pure water in kelvin.
:::
::: tab Answer 2
273.15 K, because 0 °C is 273.15 K.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 3
A thermometer in a beaker of melting pure ice reads a steady value. What is that value?
:::
::: tab Answer 3
0 °C — the melting point of pure water at standard pressure.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 4
Does dissolving salt in the ice raise or lower the observed melting point?
:::
::: tab Answer 4
It lowers it; the melting point quoted in this chapter is for pure water only.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 5
Why must the pressure be stated when quoting a melting point?
:::
::: tab Answer 5
Because the melting point is pressure dependent; the chapter's value is at standard pressure.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 6
Heat is supplied to melting ice and the temperature does not rise. Where does the energy go?
:::
::: tab Answer 6
Into the phase change — it breaks the ordered solid structure rather than raising the temperature.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 7
How much energy melts 10 g of ice already at its melting point?
:::
::: tab Answer 7
334 J/g times 10 g is 3340 J.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 8
How much energy melts 250 g of ice already at its melting point?
:::
::: tab Answer 8
334 J/g times 250 g is 83500 J.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 9
Sketch what a heating curve looks like while a pure solid melts.
:::
::: tab Answer 9
A flat plateau at the melting point, then a rise once melting is complete.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 10
Two beakers of ice are heated at different rates. Do their plateau temperatures differ?
:::
::: tab Answer 10
No — the plateau sits at the melting point regardless of the heating rate; only its duration changes.
:::
::::
